scenario: A UAE-resident company that is not a Qualifying Free Zone Person, and has not elected Small Business Relief, reports taxable income of AED 500,000 for a tax period.
prompt: Under UAE Corporate Tax Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022), what is its Corporate Tax liability for that tax period?
options: AED 11,250, applying 0% to the first AED 375,000 and 9% to the remaining AED 125,000
AED 0, because taxable income below AED 1,000,000 is fully exempt
AED 25,000, applying a flat 5% rate to the full AED 500,000
AED 45,000, applying the 9% rate to the full AED 500,000

explanation.what: UAE Corporate Tax is charged at 0% on the first AED 375,000 of taxable income and at 9% on taxable income above that.
explanation.why: Only the AED 125,000 above AED 375,000 is taxed at 9%: AED 125,000 × 9% = AED 11,250. Charging 9% on the full AED 500,000 (AED 45,000) ignores the 0% band. There is no 5% Corporate Tax rate; 5% is the VAT rate. The AED 1,000,000 figure is the turnover test for individuals' businesses, not an exemption for companies.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 3

scenario: A UAE-resident company had revenue of AED 2.8 million in both the current and the previous tax period. The current tax period starts on or after 1 June 2023 and ends on or before 31 December 2026.
prompt: Under Small Business Relief (Article 21 of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 and Ministerial Decision No. 73 of 2023), what happens if it makes a valid election for the relief for the current tax period?
options: The taxable person automatically receives Small Business Relief without needing to make any election
The taxable person is treated as if it derived no taxable income for the tax period and has no Corporate Tax liability
The taxable person still owes Corporate Tax on income above AED 375,000, because Small Business Relief only removes the registration obligation
The taxable person permanently loses eligibility for Small Business Relief in all future tax periods because its revenue is approaching the AED 3,000,000 threshold

explanation.what: A resident person whose revenue does not exceed AED 3,000,000 in the current and previous tax periods can elect Small Business Relief, and is then treated as having no taxable income for that period.
explanation.why: AED 2.8 million is under the AED 3,000,000 limit in both periods, so a valid election means no Corporate Tax for the period. The relief has to be elected; it isn't automatic. It removes the tax on the whole taxable income, not just a registration step. Being close to the limit doesn't affect eligibility unless revenue actually goes over it.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 21; Ministerial Decision No. 73 of 2023

Only the salary income, because Corporate Tax targets employment income earned above AED 1,000,000
Only the AED 1.2 million business turnover, since the AED 1,000,000 threshold is measured on licensed business or business activity turnover, and employment income is excluded from scope
Neither amount, because natural persons can never be Corporate Tax Taxable Persons under UAE law

scenario: A Qualifying Free Zone Person has total revenue of AED 80 million for a tax period. AED 3.5 million of it is Non-Qualifying Revenue.
prompt: Under the de minimis requirement for Qualifying Free Zone Persons, does this Non-Qualifying Revenue make the entity fail the test?
options: No, because AED 3.5 million is below both the AED 5 million cap and 5% of AED 80 million (AED 4 million), and the de minimis test uses whichever of those two figures is lower
Yes, because any Non-Qualifying Revenue at all disqualifies a Qualifying Free Zone Person, regardless of amount
No, because the de minimis test only applies to Free Zone Persons with total revenue below AED 50 million
Yes, because AED 3.5 million exceeds a flat AED 3 million de minimis cap that applies to every Qualifying Free Zone Person

explanation.what: A Qualifying Free Zone Person passes the de minimis test if its Non-Qualifying Revenue is no more than AED 5 million or 5% of total revenue, whichever is lower.
explanation.why: 5% of AED 80 million is AED 4 million, which is lower than AED 5 million, so the limit is AED 4 million. AED 3.5 million is under it, so the test is passed. Some Non-Qualifying Revenue is allowed; the test doesn't depend on revenue being under AED 50 million; and there is no flat AED 3 million cap.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 18; Ministerial Decision No. 265 of 2023

The 96% ownership must first be reduced to exactly 95%, since Corporate Tax Law caps eligible ownership for Tax Group purposes at that level
Each member must independently register for and pay Corporate Tax, because a Tax Group only consolidates VAT filings, not Corporate Tax
Parent Co. and Subsidiary Co. must jointly apply to the tax authority, which must approve the Tax Group before the members are treated as a single Taxable Person

explanation.why: Meeting the conditions isn't enough on its own: the group only exists once the joint application is approved. 95% is a minimum, so 96% is fine and doesn't need cutting back. And this is a Corporate Tax group under Article 40, separate from VAT grouping.

scenario: A UAE company has held 4% of a foreign company for 18 months, and paid AED 4.5 million for the shares. The foreign company is taxed at home at a statutory rate of 12%, and no more than 50% of its assets would fail the Participation Exemption's asset test.

Yes, because the AED 4 million acquisition-cost alternative to the 5% ownership test is met, and the holding-period, subject-to-tax, and asset tests are also satisfied
Yes, but only if the UAE company also elects Small Business Relief for the same tax period
No, because the subsidiary's 12% statutory tax rate is below the UAE's 9% headline Corporate Tax rate, so the subject-to-tax test fails

explanation.what: The Participation Exemption needs a holding of at least 5% or an acquisition cost of at least AED 4 million, held for 12 months, in a company taxed at 9% or more, and the asset test.
explanation.why: The AED 4.5 million cost meets the AED 4 million alternative, so a 4% holding is enough. 18 months is longer than the 12-month holding period, and 12% is above 9%, so the subject-to-tax test is met. Small Business Relief has nothing to do with it.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 23

scenario: A UAE taxable person (not a bank, insurer or individual) has Net Interest Expenditure of AED 20 million and tax-adjusted EBITDA of AED 50 million for a tax period.
prompt: Under the General Interest Deduction Limitation Rule (Article 30 of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022), how much Net Interest Expenditure can it deduct for the period?
options: AED 12 million only, because the AED 12 million de minimis figure is an absolute cap that always overrides the 30%-of-EBITDA calculation
AED 15 million (30% of the AED 50 million EBITDA), since the AED 12 million de minimis figure is a floor that does not reduce a higher EBITDA-based deduction capacity
AED 20 million in full, because the entire Net Interest Expenditure is below the taxable person's total EBITDA of AED 50 million
AED 6 million, calculated by applying 30% to the AED 20 million of Net Interest Expenditure rather than to EBITDA

explanation.what: Net Interest Expenditure is deductible up to the greater of 30% of tax-adjusted EBITDA or AED 12 million. Any excess can be carried forward.
explanation.why: 30% of AED 50 million is AED 15 million, which is more than AED 12 million, so AED 15 million is deductible and the other AED 5 million is carried forward. AED 12 million is a floor, not a cap. The 30% applies to EBITDA, not to the interest itself, and the full AED 20 million isn't allowed just because it is below total EBITDA.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 30

scenario: A UAE Taxable Person enters into an arrangement with no credible commercial or non-fiscal reason reflecting economic reality. Its main purpose, or one of its main purposes, is to reduce Corporate Tax in a way that goes against the intent of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022.

options: Nothing, because Article 50 only applies to cross-border arrangements involving a non-resident counterparty
Refer the matter exclusively to the UAE courts, since the tax authority itself has no independent power to adjust a Taxable Person's position under Article 50

Counteract the tax advantage by making a compensating adjustment, such as disallowing a deduction or recharacterising the arrangement, to reflect the transaction's true economic substance rather than its legal form
Automatically impose the maximum administrative penalty under Cabinet Decision No. 75 of 2023 without conducting any assessment or adjustment of the underlying tax position

explanation.what: Under the General Anti-Abuse Rule, where an arrangement lacks economic reality and a main purpose is a Corporate Tax advantage, the tax authority can counteract that advantage by adjusting the tax position.
explanation.why: The tax authority can make the adjustment itself, for example by disallowing a deduction or recharacterising the arrangement, without going to court first. The rule covers domestic arrangements as well as cross-border ones, and it works by correcting the tax, not by an automatic maximum penalty.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 50

scenario: Company A, a Qualifying Free Zone Person, supplies specialised software services to Company B, a Free Zone Person in the same free zone. Yes, because the recharge is made at cost with no markup, and Ministerial Decision No. 265 of 2023 treats an at-cost recharge between Free Zone Persons as automatically satisfying the Beneficial Recipient test

No, because Company B is not the Beneficial Recipient of the services: it is contractually obliged to pass their benefit on to its mainland customer. No, because a Qualifying Free Zone Person can never derive Qualifying Income from providing services to another Free Zone Person, only from selling goods

No, because Permanent Establishment status under Article 14 requires the foreign company to hold at least a 51% stake in a UAE-resident company
Yes, but only because the office employees are UAE nationals; a foreign company staffing the same office entirely with expatriate employees would not create a Permanent Establishment

explanation.why: The Dubai office is a fixed place of business used for core, ongoing work, so it is a Permanent Establishment even without a UAE branch or company. The test isn't about owning 51% of a UAE company, and the staff's nationality is irrelevant.

9%, the standard Corporate Tax rate, while the entity's genuine Qualifying Income continues to benefit from the 0% rate

scenario: A UAE-resident company's revenue was AED 3.2 million in one tax period, over the AED 3,000,000 limit, so it didn't elect Small Business Relief. In a later period its revenue falls to AED 2 million.

Yes, because eligibility is reassessed independently each tax period based solely on that period's own revenue, with no lasting effect from an earlier breach
Yes, but only if the taxable person also switches from the accrual basis to the cash basis of accounting for that later period
No, but only for the two tax periods immediately following the breach, after which eligibility is automatically restored

explanation.what: Small Business Relief needs revenue of no more than AED 3,000,000 in the current and previous periods. Once revenue goes over AED 3,000,000 in any period, the relief can't be elected in later periods.
explanation.why: The AED 3.2 million period rules the company out for good, so AED 2 million later doesn't bring it back. Eligibility isn't freshly reassessed each period, there's no two-period lock-out, and the accounting basis has nothing to do with it.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 21; Ministerial Decision No. 73 of 2023

scenario: A UAE-resident company prepares accrual-basis financial statements and has made a valid, irrevocable election to use the realisation basis. In a tax period, an investment property it holds on capital account rises in fair value by AED 300,000 (not sold), and a trade receivable on revenue account is revalued up by AED 50,000 (no cash received).
prompt: Under Article 20 of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, how are these two unrealised gains treated after the election?
options: Both amounts are excluded from taxable income until actually realised, because the realisation basis election applies uniformly to all unrealised gains regardless of how the underlying asset is classified
Both amounts remain currently taxable in full, because the realisation basis election only defers the recognition of unrealised losses, never unrealised gains
The AED 300,000 property gain remains currently taxable while the AED 50,000 receivable gain is deferred until realised, the opposite of how the election actually applies to each account

The AED 300,000 property gain is excluded from taxable income until realised, but the AED 50,000 receivable gain continues to be included in taxable income on a current basis, because the election only applies to assets and liabilities held on capital account

explanation.what: The realisation basis election defers unrealised gains and losses only on assets and liabilities held on capital account. Items on revenue account stay taxable as they arise.
explanation.why: The investment property is on capital account, so its AED 300,000 gain waits until it is realised. The receivable is on revenue account, so its AED 50,000 gain is taxed now. The election covers gains as well as losses, but it doesn't apply to everything.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 20; Corporate Tax Guide on Determination of Taxable Income (CTGDTI1)

Art 20(3) offers TWO realisation-basis elections: (a) all assets/liabilities subject to fair value or impairment accounting, or (b) only capital-account items, with revenue-account unrealised gains still taxed. Under election (a), BOTH gains are deferred (option 0). Under election (b), option 3 applies. The scenario only says 'the realisation basis', so it must state which election was made, e.g. 'elected under Article 20(3)(b) for capital-account items'. Option 3's reasoning ('the election only applies to... capital account') is also false as a general statement. meta.hold: Two defensible answers: Article 20(3) has two realisation elections; the scenario must say which was made.

scenario: A UAE-resident company has a foreign branch that is a Permanent Establishment abroad. The branch's profits are taxed there at a headline rate of 7%.
prompt: Can the company elect the Foreign Permanent Establishment exemption under Article 24 of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, so the branch's income and expenditure are left out of its UAE taxable income?
options: Yes, automatically, because any amount of foreign tax paid on the branch's profits, however low the rate, satisfies Article 24's requirements

No, because Article 24 requires a Foreign Permanent Establishment to be taxed abroad at a rate not less than 9%; a branch taxed at only 7% is a Non-Qualifying Foreign Permanent Establishment, so its income cannot be excluded through this election
Yes, but only if the company separately claims a Foreign Tax Credit for the shortfall between the 7% foreign rate and the UAE's 9% rate
No, but only because the foreign jurisdiction lacks a bilateral double-taxation treaty with the UAE, which is a precondition for any Article 24 election

explanation.what: The Foreign Permanent Establishment exemption is only for branches taxed abroad at a rate of at least 9%. A branch taxed below that can't be exempted through the election.
explanation.why: 7% is below 9%, so the branch is a Non-Qualifying Foreign Permanent Establishment and stays in the UAE tax base. Paying some foreign tax isn't enough, a Foreign Tax Credit doesn't make up the shortfall for this election, and a tax treaty isn't the test.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 24; Ministerial Decision No. 302 of 2024

The statute just says the exemption applies only to FPEs taxed at not less than 9% (Art 24(6)-(7)). Practitioner commentary (PwC) notes the 9% test may also be met if the FPE's effective rate recomputed under UAE CT rules reaches 9%. scenario: Company A transfers an asset to Company B, a member of the same Qualifying Group, under a valid Qualifying Group Relief election, at no gain or loss. Fourteen months later, Company B sells the asset to an unrelated buyer outside the group.
prompt: Under Article 26 of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, what are the Corporate Tax consequences of this sale?
options: None, because Qualifying Group Relief's clawback window is only 12 months, and 14 months has already passed since the original transfer
The clawback gain is recognised in the tax period of the original intra-group transfer, so Company A must file an amended return for that earlier period

Because the subsequent transfer outside the Qualifying Group occurs within two years of the original transfer, the clawback rule applies: the original transfer is retroactively treated as having occurred at market value on its original date, and the resulting gain or loss is recognised in the tax period of the clawback event itself
Only Company A, the original transferor, bears any clawback tax consequence; Company B's own sale of the asset to the third party is entirely disregarded for Corporate Tax purposes

explanation.what: If an asset transferred under Qualifying Group Relief leaves the group within two years, the relief is clawed back: the original transfer is treated as made at market value, with the gain or loss recognised in the period of the later event.
explanation.why: Fourteen months is inside the two-year window, so the clawback applies. The gain is recognised in the tax period of the sale, not by amending the earlier return. And Company B's sale isn't disregarded: it is taxed in the usual way.
explanation.reference: Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022, Article 26; Corporate Tax Guide on Qualifying Group Relief (CTGQGR1)

scenario: Company X transfers its whole retail division to Company Y in exchange for newly issued shares in Company Y. The relief is unaffected, because the two-year minimum holding period applies to Company Y, the transferee, rather than to Company X, the transferor that received the shares
The relief automatically converts into Qualifying Group Relief rather than being clawed back, since both companies remain UAE resident taxable persons

The relief is clawed back, because Company X disposes of the shares it received in the exchange before the two-year minimum holding period required by Article 27 has elapsed, so the original transfer is treated as having occurred at market value and the resulting gain becomes taxable

scenario: Company M borrows from its related party, Company N, and uses the money to reduce its own share capital, paying the proceeds to Company N. Company N is taxed at home at 11%.
prompt: Under the Specific Interest Deduction Limitation Rule (Article 31 of Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022), can Company M deduct the interest on this loan?
options: No, because Article 31 disallows the deduction outright with no exception, regardless of the related-party lender's own tax rate
Yes, but only because the general 30%-of-EBITDA interest limitation under Article 30 has not also been breached

Yes, because although Article 31 generally disallows interest deductions on related-party loans that fund a share-capital-reduction payment to a related party, that restriction does not apply here, since Company N is subject to tax at 11%, which is not less than the 9% rate specified in Article 3
No, because a share capital reduction funded by related-party debt is always treated as a taxable deemed dividend under UAE Corporate Tax Law regardless of Article 31
